sp.speaker: Prometheus
sp.p: Release me, Zeus; I have suffered dreadful things already.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Release you, you say—you who ought to wear heavier fetters, have the whole Caucasus piled on top of your head, and not only have your liver torn by sixteen vultures, but your eyes gouged out too, in return for molding such creatures as human beings for us, stealing fire, and fashioning women? As for how you cheated me in the division of the meat by serving up bones covered with fat while keeping the better portion for yourself, why even mention it?

sp.speaker: Prometheus
sp.p: Have I not already paid a sufficient penalty, nailed for so long a time to the Caucasus and feeding that most accursed of birds, the eagle, on my liver?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: That is not even a tiny fraction of what you ought to suffer.

sp.speaker: Prometheus
sp.p: Yet you will not release me for nothing; I will reveal to you something, Zeus, that is utterly vital.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: You are trying to trick me, Prometheus.

sp.speaker: Prometheus
sp.p: And what would I gain by that? You won't forget where the Caucasus is, nor will you run short of chains if I am caught playing tricks.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Tell me first what payment you will make that is so vital to us.

sp.speaker: Prometheus
sp.p: If I tell you where you are going right now, will you trust me when I prophesy the rest too?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Of course!

sp.speaker: Prometheus
sp.p: To Thetis, to lie with her.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: You knew that much; what comes next then? It looks as if you are going to tell the truth.

sp.speaker: Prometheus
sp.p: Have nothing to do with the Nereid, Zeus; for if she conceives a child by you, the offspring will do to you the very same thing you did—

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Do you mean I shall be cast down from my rule?

sp.speaker: Prometheus
sp.p: Heaven forbid, Zeus! Still, union with her threatens just that.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Farewell to Thetis, then! And let Hephaestus unchain you in return for this.

sp.speaker: Eros
sp.p: Even if I did do some wrong, Zeus, forgive me; I am only a child and still foolish.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: You a child, Eros—you who are far older than Iapetus? Just because you haven't grown a beard or gray hairs, on that account do you expect to be taken for a baby when you are an old and cunning rogue?

sp.speaker: Eros
sp.p: What great wrong have I done you—old man though you call me—that you even intend to put me in chains?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Consider, you accursed creature, whether it is a small thing! You make such sport of me that there is nothing you haven't turned me into—a satyr, a bull, gold, a swan, an eagle—yet you have never made a single woman fall in love with me, nor have I ever found myself pleasing to a woman through your doing; instead I have to use magic tricks on them and disguise myself, while they love the bull or the swan, and if they see me, they die of fright.

sp.speaker: Eros
sp.p: Naturally—being mortal, Zeus, they cannot bear the sight of you.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: How then do Branchus and Hyacinthus love Apollo?

sp.speaker: Eros
sp.p: Yet Daphne fled from him too, even though he has long hair and no beard. If you want to be lovable, stop shaking your aegis and carrying your thunderbolt; make yourself as sweet as possible, letting curls hang down on either side bound up with a headband, wear a purple robe, put on gilded slippers, step in rhythm to flute and tambourines, and you will see more women following you than the Maenads of Dionysus!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Get out! I wouldn't choose to be lovable at the price of becoming like that!

sp.speaker: Eros
sp.p: Then don't want to fall in love either, Zeus; that much is easy.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: No—I want to fall in love, all right, but to win them with less trouble. On those very terms I let you go.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Do you know the beautiful daughter of Inachus, Hermes?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Yes—you mean Io.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: She is no longer a girl, but a heifer.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: That is monstrous! How was she transformed?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Out of jealousy Hera changed her. And she has contrived another novel torment for the poor girl: she has set over her a many-eyed herdsman named Argus, who pastures the heifer without ever sleeping.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: What then must we do?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Fly down to Nemea—somewhere there Argus is herding—kill him, and lead Io across the sea to Egypt and make her Isis. Henceforth let her be a goddess of the people there, let her bring up the Nile, send the winds, and save sailors.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Come, Ganymede—for we have arrived where we needed to be—kiss me now, so you may see that I no longer have a hooked beak or sharp talons or wings, as I appeared to you when I seemed to be a bird.

sp.speaker: Ganymedes
sp.p: Sir, weren't you an eagle just now, and didn't you swoop down and snatch me from the middle of my flock? How have those wings fallen off you, and how have you turned into someone else already?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: You see neither a man, lad, nor an eagle; I here am the king of all the gods, who changed myself for the occasion.

sp.speaker: Ganymedes
sp.p: What do you mean? Are you that famous Pan? Then why don't you have a panpipe or horns or hairy legs?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Do you think he is the only god?

sp.speaker: Ganymedes
sp.p: Yes! And we sacrifice an uncastrated billy-goat to him, leading it to the cave where his statue stands; whereas you seem to me to be some kind of kidnapper.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Tell me, haven't you heard the name of Zeus, or seen on Gargarus the altar of him who sends rain and thunders and makes lightning?

sp.speaker: Ganymedes
sp.p:
Do you say you are the one, good sir, who poured all that hail on us the other day—the one said to live up above, who makes the noise, to whom my father sacrificed the ram?
Then what wrong did I do that you carried me off, king of the gods? Meanwhile the wolves will probably tear my sheep to pieces now, falling upon them unattended.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Do you still care about sheep now that you have become immortal and will live here with us?

sp.speaker: Ganymedes
sp.p: What are you saying? Won't you take me back down to Ida today?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Not at all—otherwise I would have turned from a god into an eagle for nothing!

sp.speaker: Ganymedes
sp.p: Then my father will look for me and be angry when he doesn't find me, and I'll get a beating later for abandoning the flock.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Where could he ever see you?

sp.speaker: Ganymedes
sp.p: Please don't—I miss him already! If you take me back, I promise you he will sacrifice another ram as a ransom for me. We have the three-year-old, the big one that leads the way to pasture.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: How innocent and simple-hearted the boy is—truly still a child!—Come, Ganymede, bid all those things farewell and forget them, both the flock and Ida. Since you are now a dweller in heaven, you will bestow many blessings from here upon both your father and your country; instead of cheese and milk you will eat ambrosia and drink nectar—indeed you yourself will pour and serve it to the rest of us too. And best of all, you will no longer be a mortal man, but will become immortal, and I will make your star shine most brightly, and in every way you will be happy.

sp.speaker: Ganymedes
sp.p: And if I want to play, who will play with me? On Ida there were many boys my own age.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Here too you have Eros here to play with you, and plenty of knucklebones. Only take heart and be cheerful, and don't pine for anything down below.

sp.speaker: Ganymedes
sp.p: What use could I be to you? Or will I have to herd sheep here too?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: No, you will be cupbearer, put in charge of the nectar, and look after the banquet.

sp.speaker: Ganymedes
sp.p: That's not hard; I know how to pour milk and hand over the wooden bowl.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Look, here he is mentioning milk again and thinking he is going to wait on humans! This is heaven, and we drink nectar, as I told you.

sp.speaker: Ganymedes
sp.p: Is it sweeter than milk, Zeus?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: You'll know in a moment, and once you've tasted it you won't miss milk anymore.

sp.speaker: Ganymedes
sp.p: And where shall I sleep at night? With my age-mate Eros?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: No—the very reason I carried you off was so that we might sleep together.

sp.speaker: Ganymedes
sp.p: Couldn't you sleep alone, then? Is it nicer for you to sleep with me?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Yes, with someone like you, Ganymede, so handsome.

sp.speaker: Ganymedes
sp.p: How will my looks help you sleep?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: They have a sweet charm and bring sleep on more softly.

sp.speaker: Ganymedes
sp.p: Actually, my father used to get annoyed with me sleeping beside him and would tell me in the morning how I ruined his sleep by tossing and turning and kicking and talking in my sleep; so he mostly sent me to sleep with my mother. It's high time, if that's why you carried me off as you say, to put me back down on earth, or you'll have trouble staying awake—I'll keep bothering you by tossing about.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p:
That is the very sweetest thing you could do for me,
if I stay awake with you, kissing and embracing you again and again.

sp.speaker: Ganymedes
sp.p: Suit yourself; I'll just sleep while you kiss me.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: We'll see then what is to be done. For now, take him away, Hermes, and once he has drunk of immortality, bring him to pour our wine, after first teaching him how to present the cup.

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: Ever since you snatched this Phrygian lad from Ida and brought him up here, Zeus, you pay less attention to me.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Are you jealous even of him now, Hera—so innocent and utterly harmless as he is? I thought you were harsh only toward the women who have anything to do with me.

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p:
Not that you behave well or decently in those affairs either, when you, master of all the gods, leave me, your lawful wife, and go down to earth to commit adultery disguised as gold or a satyr or a bull. Still, those women at least stay on earth for you, whereas you snatched up this little boy from Ida and flew back, most noble of gods, and he lives right with us, brought in over my head, supposedly to pour wine! Were you so short of cupbearers, and have Hebe and Hephaestus given up waiting at table? And you can't even take the cup from him without kissing him first in front of everyone, and his kiss is sweeter to you than nectar, which is why you often ask for a drink even when you aren't thirsty! Sometimes you just take a sip and hand it to him, and when he has drunk, you take the cup back and drink whatever is left in it from the exact spot where the boy drank and pressed his lips,
so that you may drink and kiss at the same time! And the other day the king and father of all laid aside his aegis and thunderbolt and sat playing knucklebones with him, with that huge beard hanging down! So I see all of this—don't imagine you are escaping notice.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: And what is so terrible, Hera, about kissing so handsome a lad while drinking and enjoying both the kiss and the nectar? Why, if I let him kiss you even once, you will no longer blame me for thinking his kiss preferable to nectar.

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: That is the talk of pederasts. May I never be so mad as to put my lips to this soft, effeminate Phrygian!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Don't abuse my darling, most noble lady; for this girlish, barbarian, soft boy is sweeter and more desirable to me—but I won't say it, lest I provoke you further.

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: Why don't you marry him too, for all I care! Only remember how outrageously you treat me because of this cupbearer.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: No, I suppose your son Hephaestus ought to pour our wine, limping along straight from the forge, still covered in sparks, having just put down his tongs, and we ought to take the cup from those fingers of his and draw him close to kiss him in between—a fellow whom not even you, his mother, would gladly kiss with his face blackened by soot! That's much sweeter, isn't it? Far more fitting for the gods' banquet is that cupbearer, while Ganymede must be sent back down to Ida—because he is clean and rosy-fingered and hands over the cup skillfully and, what annoys you most, kisses sweeter than nectar!

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: Now Hephaestus is lame, Zeus, and his fingers are unworthy of your cup, and he is full of soot, and you feel sick looking at him—ever since Ida reared this handsome long-haired boy! Formerly you didn't notice these things, and neither the sparks nor the forge kept you from drinking from his hand.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: You are only tormenting yourself, Hera, nothing else, and intensifying my love by your jealousy. If you dislike receiving the cup from a handsome boy, let your son pour for you; and you, Ganymede, hand the cup to me alone, and kiss me twice for every cup—both when you hand it to me full and again when you take it back from me. What's this? Are you crying? Don't be afraid; whoever tries to hurt you will regret it!

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: What sort of character do you think this Ixion is, Zeus?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: A worthy man, Hera, and good company at table; otherwise he wouldn't be dining with us if he were unworthy of the banquet.

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: Well, he is unworthy, being insolent; so let him dine with us no longer.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: What insolence did he commit? I ought to know too, I think.

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: What else?—Yet I am ashamed to say it, such is what he dared.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: All the more reason to tell it, the more shameful his attempt was. Did he make advances to someone? For I gather what sort of shameful thing you would hesitate to speak of.

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: To me myself, no one else, Zeus, for a long time now! At first I didn't understand why he kept staring intently at me; then he began sighing and shedding quiet tears, and whenever I drank and handed the cup back to Ganymede, he would ask to drink from that very same one, and taking it would kiss it as he drank, press it to his eyes, and look back at me again. By then I realized these were signs of love. For a long while I was embarrassed to tell you, thinking the man would get over his madness; but when he actually dared to make proposals to me, I left him still weeping and throwing himself at my feet, stopped up my ears so as not even to hear his insolent entreaties, and came away to tell you. Now see for yourself how you will deal with the man.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Well done, the accursed wretch—aiming at me myself, even at the bed of Hera! Has he grown so drunk on nectar? Still, we ourselves are to blame, being hospitable beyond measure in making mortals our drinking-companions. They are excusable, then, if after drinking the same drink as we and seeing heavenly beauties such as they never saw on earth, they are seized by love and desire to enjoy them. Love is a violent force, and rules not only mortals, but sometimes even us ourselves.

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: Of you indeed he is quite the absolute master, leading and dragging you around by the nose, as they say, while you follow wherever he guides you and readily change into whatever he commands—in short, you are Love's property and plaything! And now I know why you pardon Ixion: because you yourself once seduced his wife, who bore you Pirithous.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p:
Do you still remember those things—whatever little sport I had when I went down to earth? Still, do you know what I think we should do about
Ixion? Don't punish him at all or drive him from the banquet—that would be boorish; instead, since he is in love and, as you say, weeps and suffers unbearably—

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: What, Zeus? I'm afraid you're going to say something insolent too!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Not at all! Let us mold a phantom out of a cloud just like yourself, and when the banquet breaks up and he lies awake from love, as is likely, let us bring it and lay it beside him; that way he will stop tormenting himself, thinking he has attained his desire.

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: Out with him! May he come to a bad end for desiring things above his station!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Still, put up with it, Hera. What real harm could you suffer from the phantom if Ixion lies with a cloud?

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: Why, the cloud will be thought to be me, and he will commit the outrage against me because of the likeness!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: There's nothing in that: neither could the cloud ever become Hera nor you a cloud; only Ixion will be deceived.

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: Yes, but all men are vulgar; when he goes back down he will probably boast and tell everyone, claiming he lay with Hera and shares Zeus's bed, and perhaps he might even say I am in love with him, and they will believe him, not knowing he lay with a cloud.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Well then, if he says any such thing, he shall be cast into Hades, bound fast to a wheel, poor wretch, to spin around with it forever and suffer endless torment—paying the penalty not for his love (for that is nothing terrible), but for his boasting.

sp.speaker: Hephaistos
sp.p: Have you seen Maia's baby, Apollo, that was just born? How handsome he is, smiling at everyone and already showing that he will turn out to be some great blessing!

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: That baby, Hephaestus—a great blessing, when he is older than Iapetus so far as roguery goes?

sp.speaker: Hephaistos
sp.p: Why, what harm could he do, being newborn?

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: Ask Poseidon, whose trident he stole, or Ares—for he secretly drew his sword out of its sheath too—not to mention myself, whom he disarmed of my bow and arrows!

sp.speaker: Hephaistos
sp.p: That newborn did all this—the one who can barely stand, still in swaddling clothes?

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: You'll find out, Hephaestus, if he just comes near you.

sp.speaker: Hephaistos
sp.p: Actually, he already has.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: Well then? Do you have all your tools, and is none of them missing?

sp.speaker: Hephaistos
sp.p: Every single one, Apollo.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: Still, check carefully.

sp.speaker: Hephaistos
sp.p: By Zeus, I don't see my tongs!

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: Well, you'll probably find them in the baby's swaddling clothes.

sp.speaker: Hephaistos
sp.p: Is he so light-fingered, as if he had practiced thievery in the womb?

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p:
Yes, for you haven't heard him chattering away already, glib and fluent—and he wants to be our attendant too! Yesterday he challenged Eros and instantly threw him in wrestling by tripping his feet somehow; then, while he was being praised, he stole Aphrodite's girdle as she hugged
him for his victory, and while Zeus was still laughing he took his scepter! If the thunderbolt hadn't been too heavy and full of fire, he would have stolen that too.

sp.speaker: Hephaistos
sp.p: You describe a spirited child!

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: Not only that, he is already a musician too.

sp.speaker: Hephaistos
sp.p: From what can you tell that?

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: He found a dead tortoise somewhere and fashioned an instrument out of it: fitting arms to it and joining a crossbar, then fixing pegs and setting a bridge underneath and stretching seven strings, he played a most refined and harmonious melody, Hephaestus—so much so that even I envied him, long as I have practiced the lyre! And Maia said he doesn't even stay in heaven at night, but out of curiosity goes all the way down to Hades—obviously to steal something from there too. He has wings as well, and has made himself a rod of marvelous power with which he guides souls and leads down the dead.

sp.speaker: Hephaistos
sp.p: I gave him that rod to be a toy.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: Well, he paid you back your wage—your tongs—

sp.speaker: Hephaistos
sp.p: Good thing you reminded me! I'll go right now to get them back, in case they turn up in his swaddling clothes as you say.

sp.speaker: Hephaistos
sp.p: What must I do, Zeus? I have come as you ordered, bringing my sharpest axe, even if a stone needs to be split with a single blow.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Good, Hephaestus! Now bring it down and split my head in two.

sp.speaker: Hephaistos
sp.p: Are you testing me to see if I'm mad? Come, give me some other order for whatever you really want done.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: This very thing—to split my skull! If you disobey, it won't be the first time you experience my anger. Strike with all your might and don't delay; I am dying of labor pains that are turning my brain upside down!

sp.speaker: Hephaistos
sp.p: Careful, Zeus, lest we do some mischief; the axe is sharp and will not act as midwife for you bloodlessly or in the manner of Eileithyia.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Just strike boldly, Hephaestus; I know what is best.

sp.speaker: Hephaistos
sp.p: Unwillingly, yet I will strike—what else can one do when you command? What's this? An armed maiden! A great trouble you had in your head, Zeus! No wonder you were quick-tempered, breeding so big a virgin under your skull-membrane, and in full armor at that! You had a military camp, not a head, without knowing it! Look, she leaps and dances the war-dance, shakes her shield, brandishes her spear, and is filled with divine frenzy—and best of all, she has grown very beautiful and in full bloom already in an instant! Gray-eyed, to be sure, yet even that is set off by her helmet. So, Zeus, pay me my midwife's fee by betrothing her to me right now!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: You ask what is impossible, Hephaestus; she will choose to remain a virgin forever. For my own part, however, I raise no objection.

sp.speaker: Hephaistos
sp.p: That's all I wanted! I'll take care of the rest, and I'll seize her right now.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: If you find it easy, go ahead; though I know you are enamored of impossibilities.

sp.speaker: Poseidon
sp.p: May one see Zeus now, Hermes?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Not at all, Poseidon.

sp.speaker: Poseidon
sp.p: Announce me to him anyway.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Don't bother him, I tell you; it is not the right time, so you cannot see him at present.

sp.speaker: Poseidon
sp.p: Is he with Hera?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: No, it is something quite different.

sp.speaker: Poseidon
sp.p: I understand—Ganymede is inside.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Not that either; he himself is unwell.

sp.speaker: Poseidon
sp.p: How so, Hermes? That is strange news you tell.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: I am embarrassed to say, it is of such a nature.

sp.speaker: Poseidon
sp.p: You shouldn't be with me, your uncle!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: He has just given birth, Poseidon.

sp.speaker: Poseidon
sp.p: Nonsense! He gave birth? By whom? So he was a hermaphrodite without our knowing it? Yet his belly showed no swelling at all.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: You're right—his belly didn't hold the embryo.

sp.speaker: Poseidon
sp.p: I know! He gave birth from his head again, like Athena—he has a fertile head!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: No, he was carrying Semele's baby in his thigh.

sp.speaker: Poseidon
sp.p: Bravo to the noble fellow! How pregnant he is all over, in every part of his body! But who is Semele?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: A Theban woman, one of Cadmus's daughters. He lay with her and got her with child.

sp.speaker: Poseidon
sp.p: And then he gave birth in her place, Hermes?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p:
Indeed he did, paradoxical as it seems to you. Hera—you know how jealous she is—insinuated herself into Semele's confidence and persuaded her to ask Zeus to come to her with thunder
and lightning. When he agreed and came bringing his thunderbolt as well, the roof caught fire and Semele perished in the flames; he ordered me to cut open the woman's womb and bring him the still unfinished seven-month fetus. When I had done so, he split open his own thigh and put it inside to come to full term there; and now in the third month he has delivered it and is weak from the labor pains.

sp.speaker: Poseidon
sp.p: Where is the baby now, then?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: I carried him off to Nysa and gave him to the Nymphs to rear, named Dionysus.

sp.speaker: Poseidon
sp.p: So our brother is both mother and father to this Dionysus?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: So it seems. Anyway, I'm off to bring him water for his wound and do the other things customary for a woman in childbed.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Helios, Zeus says not to drive out today, nor tomorrow, nor the day after, but to stay indoors, and let the time in between be one long night; so let the Hours unharness the horses again, and you put out your fire and take a long rest.

sp.speaker: Helios
sp.p: Strange and unheard-of orders you bring, Hermes! Did I seem to go off course in my run and drive outside the boundaries, so that he is angry with me and has decided to make the night three times as long as the day?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Nothing of the sort, nor will this be forever; he just needs the night to be somewhat longer for himself right now.

sp.speaker: Helios
sp.p: Where is he, then, and from where were you sent to bring me this message?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: From Boeotia, Helios, from Amphitryon's wife, whom he is visiting because he is in love with her.

sp.speaker: Helios
sp.p: Isn't one night enough, then?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Not at all—a great god of many labors must be begotten from this union, and it is impossible to finish him in a single night.

sp.speaker: Helios
sp.p: Well, good luck to him in finishing his work! Still, Hermes, such things did not happen in Cronus's time—we are alone here—nor did he ever sleep away from Rhea or leave heaven to spend the night in Thebes; instead, day was day and night kept its proper measure according to the seasons, with nothing strange or out of order, nor would he ever have had anything to do with a mortal woman! Whereas now, for the sake of a wretched little woman, everything must be turned upside down, my horses must grow stiff from idleness, the road must become hard to travel from going untrodden three days in a row, and mortals must live miserably in darkness! That's the benefit they'll get from Zeus's love affairs—sitting and waiting in prolonged gloom until he finishes this champion you speak of!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Hush, Helios, lest you suffer for your words! I am off to Selene and Sleep to deliver Zeus's instructions to them as well: she is to proceed slowly, and Sleep is not to release mortals, so they won't realize the night has grown so long.

sp.speaker: Aphrodite
sp.p: What is this they say you are doing, Selene? That whenever you are over Caria, you halt your team to gaze down at Endymion sleeping in the open air like the hunter he is, and sometimes even descend to him in the middle of your journey?

sp.speaker: Selenes
sp.p: Ask your son, Aphrodite, who is to blame for this.

sp.speaker: Aphrodite
sp.p: Oh, he is an insolent boy! Look what he has done even to me, his own mother—now bringing me down to Ida for Anchises of Troy, now to Lebanon for that Assyrian lad, whom he also made lovable to Persephone and so robbed me of half my darling! So I have often threatened that if he doesn't stop doing such things, I'll break his bow and quiver and strip off his wings as well; and I've even spanked his bottom with my sandal! Yet somehow, though he is frightened and begs for mercy at the moment, a little later he has forgotten all about it.

sp.speaker: Aphrodite
sp.p: Still, tell me, is Endymion handsome? For that makes the misfortune easy to bear.

sp.speaker: Selenes
sp.p: To me he seems utterly handsome, Aphrodite, especially when he spreads his cloak on the rock and sleeps with his javelins in his left hand already slipping from his grasp, while his right arm is bent up around his head, framing his face gracefully, and relaxed in sleep he breathes out that ambrosial breath. Then I come down silently, stepping on tiptoe so he won't wake up and be startled—you know the rest; why should I tell you what follows? Only this: I am dying of love!

sp.speaker: Aphrodite
sp.p: My child Eros, see what you are doing! I don't mean on earth—all the things you persuade mortals to do against themselves or one another—but even in heaven: you make a spectacle of Zeus in many shapes, changing him into whatever suits you at the moment; you bring Selene down from the sky; you sometimes force Helios to linger with Clymene, forgetting his chariot-driving; and as for the outrages you commit against me, your mother, you do them boldly enough. Now, you reckless creature, you have even persuaded Rhea herself, old woman and mother of so many gods though she is, to fall in love with a boy and pine for that Phrygian lad! And now she has gone mad because of you: yoking her lions and taking along the Corybantes, who are just as crazed themselves, they roam up and down Ida, she shrieking over Attis, while among the Corybantes one slashes his forearm with a sword, another lets his hair loose and rushes madly through the mountains, another blows on a horn, another booms on a tambourine or clashes a cymbal—in short, everything on Ida is uproar and madness! So I am terrified of everything—I who gave birth to such a pest as you—terrified that Rhea in a fit of madness, or rather while still in her senses, may order the Corybantes to seize you and tear you limb from limb or throw you to the lions! That is what I fear when I see the danger you are in.

sp.speaker: Eros
sp.p:
Take heart, Mother, for I am already on friendly terms with the lions themselves! I often climb onto their backs, grab their manes, and drive them, and they wag their tails at me, take my hand in their mouths, lick it all over, and give it back. As for Rhea herself, when would
she ever have time for me, absorbed as she is in Attis? Besides, what wrong do I do by showing beautiful things as they are? You should simply stop desiring what is beautiful—so don't blame me for it! Or would you yourself like to stop being in love, Mother—neither you with Ares nor he with you?

sp.speaker: Aphrodite
sp.p: How clever you are, and you master everyone! Still, one day you will remember my words.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Stop quarreling with each other like mortals, Asclepius and Heracles! This is unseemly and out of place at the banquet of the gods.

sp.speaker: Herakles
sp.p: Do you really want this druggist, Zeus, to recline above me?

sp.speaker: Asklepios
sp.p: By Zeus, yes—for I am the better man!

sp.speaker: Herakles
sp.p: In what respect, you thunderstruck fool? Because Zeus struck you with a thunderbolt for doing what was forbidden, and now out of pity you have been granted immortality again?

sp.speaker: Asklepios
sp.p: Have you forgotten that you too were burned to ashes on Oeta, Heracles, that you reproach me with fire?

sp.speaker: Herakles
sp.p: Our lives are not at all equal or alike! I am Zeus's son and have performed so many labors cleansing human life, conquering monsters and punishing insolent men; whereas you are a root-cutter and a quack—useful perhaps to sick people for applying poultices, but having never shown a single manly deed!

sp.speaker: Asklepios
sp.p:
Well said—considering I healed your burns when you came up here the other day half-roasted, your body ruined by both the tunic and then the fire! For my part, if nothing else, I never served as a slave like you, nor
carded wool in Lydia dressed in a purple robe and beaten by Omphale with a golden sandal, nor did I go mad and kill my wife and children!

sp.speaker: Herakles
sp.p: If you don't stop abusing me, you'll find out right away that your immortality won't help you much—I'll pick you up and throw you headlong out of heaven, so that not even Paeon will be able to heal your smashed skull!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Stop it, I say, and don't disturb our gathering, or I'll send both of you away from the banquet! Still, it is reasonable, Heracles, for Asclepius to recline above you, seeing that he died first.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Why so gloomy, Apollo?

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: Because I am unlucky in love, Hermes.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: That is certainly cause for grief. What is your misfortune? Does the affair with Daphne still trouble you?

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: Not at all—I am mourning my Laconian darling, the son of Oebalus.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Tell me, is Hyacinthus dead?

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: Yes, indeed.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: By whose hand, Apollo? Who was so unfeeling as to kill that handsome lad?

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: It was my own doing.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Did you go mad, Apollo?

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: No, it was an involuntary accident.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: How? I want to hear how it happened.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p:
He was learning to throw the discus, and I was throwing with him; now Zephyrus, most accursed of winds, had long been in love with him too, and being neglected and unable to bear the slight—when I tossed the discus up into the air as we were accustomed to do, he blew down from Taygetus and drove it straight onto the boy's head,
so that from the blow much blood flowed and the boy died on the spot. I took revenge on Zephyrus at once, shooting him with my arrows and pursuing him as he fled all the way to the mountain; for the boy I raised a burial mound at Amyclae where the discus struck him down, and from his blood I caused the earth to send up a flower, the sweetest and fairest of all flowers, Hermes, still bearing letters that lament the dead boy. Do you think I grieve without reason?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Yes, Apollo—you knew you had taken a mortal as your darling, so don't be upset that he died.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: To think that he—lame and a blacksmith by trade, Apollo—has married the two loveliest goddesses, Aphrodite and Charis!

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: A stroke of good luck, Hermes; still, what I marvel at is that they can bear living with him, especially when they see him streaming with sweat, hunched over the forge, with thick soot on his face! Yet even so they embrace him, kiss him, and sleep with him.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: That is what annoys me too, and makes me envy Hephaestus! Go ahead, Apollo, wear your long hair, play your lyre, and be proud of your beauty, and I'll be proud of my fine physique and my lyre—and then when bedtime comes, we'll sleep alone!

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p:
For my part, I am generally unlucky in
love anyway: of the two I loved most, Daphne and Hyacinthus, Daphne hated me so much she chose to become a tree rather than be with me, and Hyacinthus I lost to the discus—so now instead of them I have garlands!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Well, I did once have Aphrodite—but one mustn't boast.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: I know, and she is said to have borne Hermaphroditus to you. Still, tell me this, if you know: why isn't Aphrodite jealous of Charis, or Charis of her?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Because, Apollo, Charis lives with him on Lemnos, whereas Aphrodite is in heaven; besides, she is mostly occupied with Ares and is in love with him, so she cares little about this blacksmith.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: And do you think Hephaestus knows this?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: He knows; but what could he do, seeing that Ares is a strapping young man and a soldier? So he keeps quiet—though he does threaten to contrive some kind of chains for them and catch them in a net on the bed.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: I don't know—I'd wish to be the one caught myself!

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: Fine children indeed you bore to Zeus, Leto!

sp.speaker: Leto
sp.p: Not all of us, Hera, can bear such children as Hephaestus!

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p:
Well, lame though he is, he is useful at least, being an excellent craftsman who has adorned heaven for us, married Aphrodite, and is cherished by
her; whereas as for your children, one of them is unfemininely masculine and haunts the mountains, and most recently has gone off to Scythia where everyone knows what she eats, slaughtering strangers and imitating the Scythians themselves, who are cannibals! And Apollo pretends to know everything—archery, lyre-playing, medicine, and prophecy—and having set up prophecy workshops at Delphi, Claros, and Didyma, he deceives those who consult him by giving crooked, ambiguous answers that fit either side of the question, so there is no risk of being wrong! He grows rich from this, of course, since fools are plentiful and let themselves be hoodwinked; yet the more sensible people are well aware that most of it is charlatanry. Why, the prophet himself didn't know he was going to kill his darling with the discus, nor did he foresee that Daphne would flee from him, handsome and long-haired though he is! So I fail to see how you were thought to have finer children than Niobe.

sp.speaker: Leto
sp.p: Yet I know how it pains you to see these very children—the slayer of strangers and the false prophet—among the gods, especially when she is praised for her beauty and he plays the lyre at the banquet to everyone's admiration.

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: You make me laugh, Leto! Him admirable—whom Marsyas would have flayed after beating him in music, if the Muses had been willing to judge fairly! As it was, the poor fellow was cheated and perished after an unjust verdict. And your pretty virgin is so pretty that when she learned Actaeon had seen her, afraid the young man would tell everyone how ugly she was, she set her hounds on him! Not to mention that she wouldn't even be acting as midwife to women in labor if she were truly a virgin herself!

sp.speaker: Leto
sp.p:
You are proud, Hera, because you live with Zeus and
share his throne, and so you hand out insults without fear; yet I shall soon see you weeping again, whenever he leaves you and goes down to earth turned into a bull or a swan.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: Why are you laughing, Hermes?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Because I saw the most hilarious sight, Apollo!

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: Tell me then, so I can hear it and laugh along with you.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Aphrodite has been caught in bed with Ares, and Hephaestus captured them and tied them up!

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: How? It sounds like you have a delightful story to tell.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Knowing about it for a long time, I suppose, he lay in wait for them; he arranged invisible chains around the bed and went off to work at his forge. Then Ares slipped in unseen, as he thought, but Helios spotted him and told Hephaestus. Once they climbed into bed, got to work, and were inside the net, the chains wrapped around them and Hephaestus walked in! She—being naked, of course—had no way to cover herself in her shame, while Ares at first tried to escape, hoping to break the chains, and then, realizing he was trapped beyond escape, began begging for mercy.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: Well? Did Hephaestus untie them?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Not yet! Instead he called the gods together and is showing off the adultery to them. There they both are, naked, heads bowed, tied together and blushing—and the sight seemed utterly delightful to me, almost like watching the act itself!

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: Isn't that blacksmith ashamed to put his own marital disgrace on display?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p:
By Zeus, no—he's standing over them laughing!
For my part, to tell the truth, I envied Ares not only for committing adultery with the loveliest goddess, but even for being tied up with her!

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: So you'd even put up with being tied up on those terms?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Wouldn't you, Apollo? Just go and look—I'll congratulate you if you don't wish the same for yourself when you see them!

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: I would be ashamed, Zeus, if I had such a son—so effeminate and ruined by drunkenness, his hair bound up with a headband, spending most of his time with frenzied women, softer than they are themselves, dancing to tambourines, flute, and cymbals—in short, resembling anyone rather than you, his father.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Yet this very headband-wearing fellow, softer than women, not only subdued Lydia, Hera, captured the dwellers on Mount Tmolus, and brought the Thracians under his sway, but marched against the Indians with that womanish army of his, took their elephants, conquered their land, and led away captive their king who dared to resist for a moment—and he did all this while dancing and leaping, using ivy-wreathed thyrsi, drunk, as you say, and inspired! And if anyone tried to revile him by insulting his rites, he punished him too, either binding him with vine-shoots or having him torn to pieces like a fawn by his own mother. Do you see how manly these deeds are, and not unworthy of his father? If playfulness and luxury go along with them, there is no harm in that—especially if one considers what he would be like sober, when he accomplishes this much while drunk!

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: Next you look ready to praise his invention too—the vine and wine—even though you see what drunkards do, staggering about, turning to violence, and going utterly mad from drink! Why, Icarius, to whom he first gave the vine-shoot, was killed by his own drinking-companions beating him with mattocks!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: There's nothing in that: neither wine nor Dionysus causes such things, but immoderate drinking and guzzling unmixed wine beyond what is proper. Whoever drinks in moderation becomes more cheerful and pleasant, and would never do to any fellow drinker what happened to Icarius. No, you still seem to be jealous, Hera, and to remember Semele, when you slander Dionysus's finest achievements.

sp.speaker: Aphrodite
sp.p: Why on earth, Eros, have you conquered all the other gods—Zeus, Poseidon, Apollo, Rhea, and me your mother—yet you keep away from Athena alone, and against her your torch has no fire, your quiver is empty of arrows, and you are without bow or aim?

sp.speaker: Eros
sp.p: I am afraid of her, Mother! She is terrifying, fierce-eyed, and dreadfully mannish; whenever I draw my bow and advance on her, she shakes her helmet-crest and scares me so that I start trembling and my arrows slip right out of my hands.

sp.speaker: Aphrodite
sp.p: Wasn't Ares even more terrifying? Yet you disarmed and defeated him.

sp.speaker: Eros
sp.p:
Yes, but he welcomes me willingly and invites me in, whereas Athena always eyes me with suspicion; once I just happened
to fly past nearby with my torch, and she said, "If you come near me, by my father, I'll run you through with my spear, or grab you by the foot and hurl you into Tartarus, or tear you apart myself and make an end of you!" Many such threats she made; besides, she has a piercing gaze, and on her chest she wears a frightful face with vipers for hair, which I fear most of all—it scares me like a bogeyman and I run away whenever I see it!

sp.speaker: Aphrodite
sp.p: Well, you are afraid of Athena, as you say, and of the Gorgon—even though you didn't fear Zeus's thunderbolt. But why are the Muses unwounded by you and out of range of your shafts? Do they shake helmet-crests and display Gorgons too?

sp.speaker: Eros
sp.p: I respect them, Mother; they are august, always deep in thought and devoted to song, and I often stand beside them charmed by their melody.

sp.speaker: Aphrodite
sp.p: Leave them alone too, then, since they are august. But why don't you wound Artemis?

sp.speaker: Eros
sp.p: First of all, it isn't even possible to catch her, always fleeing through the mountains; besides, she is already in love with a passion of her own.

sp.speaker: Aphrodite
sp.p: With what, my child?

sp.speaker: Eros
sp.p: Hunting, stags, and fawns—chasing them down and shooting them with arrows; she is completely absorbed in that. For as to her brother, even though he is an archer too and a far-shooter—

sp.speaker: Aphrodite
sp.p: I know, my child—you have shot him many a time!

div.head: The Judgment of the Goddesses This is listed as a separate work, The Council of the Gods

sp.speaker: Ares
sp.p: Did you hear what Zeus threatened us with, Hermes—how arrogant and unbelievable? "If I wish," he says, "I will let down a chain from heaven, and you can hang onto it and try with all your might to pull me down, yet you will toil in vain, for you will never drag me down; whereas if I should wish to pull up, I will haul up and suspend not only you, but earth and sea together with you!"—and all the rest that you heard too. Now I wouldn't deny that he is better and stronger than any one of us individually, but that he surpasses all of us together so that we couldn't overpower him even if we added earth and sea to our weight—I could never be convinced of that!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p:
Watch your tongue, Ares! It isn't safe to say
such things, lest we suffer some harm for our loose talk.

sp.speaker: Ares
sp.p: Do you think I would say this to everyone, and not just to you alone, whom I knew could keep a secret? Anyway, what struck me as most laughable as I listened to his threat I simply can't keep quiet about to you: I remember not long ago, when Poseidon, Hera, and Athena rose up and plotted to seize and bind him, how frantic with terror he was—against just three of them!—and if Thetis hadn't taken pity on him and summoned the hundred-handed Briareus as his ally, he would have been tied up, thunderbolt, thunder, and all! Remembering that, I couldn't help laughing at his fine speeches.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Be quiet, I say! It is safe neither for you to speak nor for me to hear such things.

sp.speaker: Pan
sp.p: Greetings, Father Hermes!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Greetings to you too. Wait—how am I your father?

sp.speaker: Pan
sp.p: Aren't you Cyllenian Hermes?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Indeed I am. How then are you my son?

sp.speaker: Pan
sp.p: I am a love-child, begotten by you out of wedlock.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: By Zeus, of some billy-goat committing adultery with a she-goat, perhaps! How could you be mine, with horns, a nose like that, a shaggy beard, cloven goat-legs, and a tail above your rump?

sp.speaker: Pan
sp.p: Whatever taunts you throw at me, your own son, Father, you bring disgrace on me—or rather on yourself, for begetting and fathering such offspring; I am not to blame!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Who do you say your mother is, then? Did I somehow commit adultery with a she-goat without realizing it?

sp.speaker: Pan
sp.p: You didn't commit adultery with a she-goat; just recall whether you once forced a freeborn maiden in Arcadia. Why are you biting your finger and racking your brains in perplexity? I mean Penelope, daughter of Icarius!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Then what came over her to bear you looking like a goat instead of me?

sp.speaker: Pan
sp.p: I'll give you her very own words! When she sent me off to Arcadia, she said: "My child, I am your mother, Spartan Penelope, and know that you have as your father the god Hermes, son of Maia and Zeus. If you have horns and goat-legs, let it not grieve you; for when your father lay with me, he disguised himself as a goat so as not to be recognized, and that is why you turned out like a goat."

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: By Zeus, I do remember doing something of the sort! So I, who pride myself on my beauty and am still beardless myself, am to be called your father and become a laughingstock to everyone for my fine offspring?

sp.speaker: Pan
sp.p: Yet I won't disgrace you, Father! I am musical and play the panpipe with a very crisp tone, and Dionysus can do nothing without me, but has made me his companion and fellow reveler, and I lead his chorus; and if you saw my flocks, all the ones I have around Tegea and over Mount Parthenium, you would be delighted! I rule all of Arcadia too; and recently, fighting alongside the Athenians, I acquitted myself so nobly at Marathon that a prize of valor was voted to me—the cave beneath the Acropolis! If you go to Athens, you'll see how great the name of Pan is there.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Tell me, Pan—that's what they call you, I think—are you married yet?

sp.speaker: Pan
sp.p: Not at all, Father; I am amorous and couldn't be content living with just one.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: So you make advances to the she-goats, obviously.

sp.speaker: Pan
sp.p: You may mock, but I have Echo and Pitys and all of Dionysus's Maenads, and I am very much sought after by them!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Do you know, my child, what first favor you can grant me?

sp.speaker: Pan
sp.p: Command me, Father; we will see to it.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Come visit me and be friendly—only make sure you never call me "Father" within anyone else's hearing!

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: What can we say, Dionysus, to the fact that Eros, Hermaphroditus, and Priapus are brothers by the same mother, yet utterly unlike in form and habits? The first is wholly beautiful, an archer, and invested with no small power, ruling over all; the second is effeminate, half-man, and ambiguous in appearance—you couldn't tell whether he is a youth or a maiden; and the third, Priapus, is masculine beyond all decency!

sp.speaker: Dionysos
sp.p: Don't be surprised, Apollo; Aphrodite is not the reason for this, but their different fathers—considering that even children of the same father from a single womb are often born one male and one female, just like you and your sister.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: Yes, but we look alike and follow the same pursuits—we are both archers.

sp.speaker: Dionysos
sp.p: Up to the bow you are the same, Apollo, but in other respects you aren't alike: Artemis slaughters strangers among the Scythians, while you prophesy and heal the sick.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: Do you think my sister enjoys being with the Scythians, when she is all ready, if any Greek ever arrives in Tauris, to sail away with him, loathing those sacrifices?

sp.speaker: Dionysos
sp.p: Good for her! As for Priapus, though—I'll tell you a funny story: recently when I was in Lampsacus, I was passing by the city and he welcomed me and entertained me at his house; after we went to rest following the banquet, well-soaked with wine, right around midnight the fine fellow got up—I'm embarrassed to say it.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: He made a pass at you, Dionysus?

sp.speaker: Dionysos
sp.p: Something like that.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: And what did you do about it?

sp.speaker: Dionysos
sp.p: What else could I do but laugh?

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: Well done, not taking it harshly or angrily! He is excusable, after all, for making a pass at someone as handsome as you.

sp.speaker: Dionysos
sp.p: On that score, Apollo, he might try it on you too— you're so handsome and long-haired that Priapus would make an attempt on you even when sober!

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: Oh, he won't try it, Dionysus—along with my long hair, I have my bow!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Is there any god in heaven more miserable than I am, Mother?

sp.speaker: Maia
sp.p: Don't say any such thing, Hermes.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p:
Why shouldn't I say it, when I have so much trouble, toiling all alone and torn in pieces by so many chores? At dawn I have to get up and sweep the banquet hall, spread the couches, tidy everything up, and then wait
on Zeus and carry his messages up and down all day like a courier; and when I get back, still covered in dust, I have to serve the ambrosia—and before this newly bought cupbearer arrived, I used to pour the nectar too! Worst of all, I alone of all the gods don't even sleep at night, because even then I have to escort souls for Pluto, act as conductor of the dead, and attend the court! As if my daytime duties weren't enough—being in the wrestling-schools, acting as herald in assemblies, and training orators—I still have to be split in two to help run the business of the dead!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Yet Leda's two sons spend alternate days in heaven and in Hades, whereas I have to do both jobs every single day! And the sons of Alcmene and Semele, born of wretched mortal women, feast without a care, while I, son of Maia daughter of Atlas, wait on them! And just now, the moment I got back from Sidon from Cadmus's daughter—where he sent me to see what the girl is doing—without even letting me catch my breath he has sent me off again to Argos to check on Danaë; "and then from there," he says, "go to Boeotia and on the way take a look at Antiope!" I am completely worn out! Honestly, if it were possible, I would gladly ask to be sold to a new master, like slaves on earth who are badly treated.

sp.speaker: Maia
sp.p: Never mind that, my child; you must obey your father in everything while you are young. Now hurry off to Argos as you were sent, and then to Boeotia, lest you get a beating for dawdling—lovers are quick-tempered!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p:
What have you done, worst of Titans? You have ruined everything on earth by entrusting your chariot to a foolish boy,
who burned up some regions by driving close to the ground, caused others to perish from cold by drawing the fire far away from them, and in short threw everything into confusion and chaos—and if I hadn't realized what was happening and struck him down with my thunderbolt, not a remnant of mankind would have survived! What a fine charioteer and driver you sent out for us!

sp.speaker: Helios
sp.p: I did wrong, Zeus, yet do not be angry that I gave in to my son's many entreaties; how could I ever have expected so great a disaster to happen?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Didn't you know how much precision the task required, and that if someone strayed even slightly from the road, everything is lost? And didn't you know the spirit of your horses, how firmly one must hold the bit? If anyone slacks off, they bolt immediately—just as they ran away with him, now to the left, a moment later to the right, sometimes in the opposite direction of the course, and up and down, wherever they pleased; and he had no idea how to handle them.

sp.speaker: Helios
sp.p:
I knew all of that, and for that reason I resisted for a long time and wouldn't trust him with the driving; but when he begged me in tears, and his mother Clymene along with him, I helped him onto the chariot and instructed him how to stand, how far upward to let them go before turning, then how to incline downward again, and how to keep firm control of the reins and not give in to the horses' temper; I also told him how great the danger was if he didn't drive straight. But he—being a boy—once he mounted such a blazing fire and looked down into the yawning abyss, was naturally terrified; and when the horses sensed it wasn't me aboard, despising the lad they swerved off the road and caused all this havoc, while he let go of the reins—afraid of falling out himself, I suppose—and clung to the chariot rail.
Still, he has already paid the penalty, and my grief, Zeus, is enough.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: "Enough," you say, after daring such a thing? Well, for now I pardon you, but in the future, if you break the law like this again or send out any such substitute for yourself, you shall learn at once how much hotter my thunderbolt is than your fire! So let his sisters bury him beside the Eridanus where he fell from the chariot, weeping amber over him, and let them become poplars in their grief; as for you, mend your chariot—for the pole is broken and one of the wheels is smashed—hitch up the horses, and drive! And remember all of this.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: Can you tell me, Hermes, which of these two is Castor and which is Pollux? For I couldn't tell them apart.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: The one who was with us yesterday was Castor, and this one is Pollux.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: How do you tell? They look identical.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Because this one, Apollo, has the marks of wounds on his face that he got from his opponents in boxing, especially all the ones he received from the Bebrycian Amycus when sailing with Jason; whereas the other shows nothing of the sort, but has a clear and unscarred face.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p:
You've done me a favor by teaching me the distinguishing marks, since everything else is identical—the half-eggshell, the star above, the javelin in hand, and a white horse for each—
so that I have often addressed the one as Castor when he was Pollux, and the other by Pollux's name! Now tell me this too: why on earth aren't both of them with us together, instead of taking half-shares so that each is now a dead man, now a god?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: They do this out of brotherly love; since one of Leda's sons had to die and one be immortal, they divided immortality between themselves in this way.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: Not a very clever division, Hermes, since this way they won't even see each other, which I suppose is what they wanted most! How could they, when one is among the gods and the other among the dead? Anyway, just as I prophesy, Asclepius heals, you teach wrestling as an expert trainer, Artemis acts as midwife, and each of the others has some skill useful to gods or mortals, what will these two do for us? Or will they just feast idly, big fellows as they are?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Not at all—they have been assigned to serve Poseidon: they must ride over the sea, and if they see sailors caught in a storm anywhere, alight upon the ship and save those aboard.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: A noble and saving craft you describe, Hermes!
